“Yesterday’s Newsreel” is a 1950’s made for television series comprised of vintage newsreel footage and modern narration. The series was produced by the short lived ZIV TV network using the holdings of the General Newsreel Company. Episodes ran for 12 minutes covering a variety of topics including news, fashion, sports and politics providing modern viewers with a glimpse into global history. The compilation is broken into segments beginning with the final emperor of Germany; Wilhelm II’s exile into the Netherlands at the close of WWI. Other portions feature the 1933 Chesapeake-Potomac hurricane’s devastation along the east coast and the demobilization of WWI troops as patriotic celebrations erupt in New York for the return of the ‘Fighting 69th.” Footage captures WWI soldiers, artillery, Woodrow Wilson, gyroplanes and the historic steamship; the “Grand Republic.” 

0:00 Title screen (:23) and the ZIV TV logo. “Emperor into Exile” (:40) opens with Wilhelm II and his wife, Hermine Reuss of Griez (:49). Wilhelm reigned as Kaiser from 1888 until his abdication on November 9th 1918 following a series of military defeats. His reign fell with the collapse of the German war effort leading to the end of the German monarchy. Wilhelm was exiled to the Netherlands. The Dutch government granted him asylum and refused to submit to Allied demands to extradite him as a war criminal. He and Hermine greet military officials (1:05). German soldiers march down a lightly wooded trail (1:22) for group photographs (1:34). Soldiers move down city streets (1:54). The German Calvary follows (2:01). Wilhelm walks a dog near street cars parked along the curb (2:30). A large caliber railway guns fires (3:20). The cavalry runs supplies over embankments (3:29). Soldiers fire rounds off trench mortars (3:33), man cannons (3:41) and run crates of ammunition (3:47). Woodrow Wilson and wife Edith Bolling watch US troops pass in review (3:52). Aviation history features a gyroplane (4:47) on ground and in the air (4:57). German flags wave during a Berlin march (5:15). A section from 1924 (5:32) features an automobile race (5:37). Drivers run through rural portions of an unidentified town (6:00). The trophy winner celebrates (6:22). Personalities of 1928 (6:25) highlights Arne Borg (6:45); the Swedish swimmer. Arne broke 32 world records and won 5 Olympic medals. In 1933 (8:10), the Chesapeake-Potomac Hurricane struck the north eastern US coast most notably Maryland’s Ocean City, Ocean View, Virginia and fishing piers of New Jersey. Footage opens with rescue efforts (8:16) and houses in flood waters (8:25). A man swims for a window in a drowning house (8:28). A Ford Model T drives past a tipped over bus (8:44). Rough sea waters blow up a passenger liner’s hull (8:56). Erosion along the beaches sunk beachfront properties in sand (9:05). Porches appear slumped (9:10). A local shovels out a Model T from sand (9:12). Footage highlights damaged boardwalks (9:16) piers (9:27). A pair stand atop a ruined train (9:36). April of 1919 saw the return of the famed “Fighting 69th” regiment to New York City following active duty tours in Germany during WWI (10:01). The troops were a part of the 42nd (Rainbow) Division. US flags wave frantically as troop bearing ships make way for New York harbors (10:10-10:52). The “Grand Republic;” the largest steamboat ever constructed for excursion purposes exclusively in the port of New York, appears (11:18). Ferries cart troops inland (11:24). This restricted police instructional film "Vehicle Ambush Counter Attacks" (1975) presents a detailed series of simulated terrorist vehicle ambushes and defensive driving responses. It focuses heavily on roadblocks, rolling ambushes, vehicle ramming, emergency braking, escaping over curbs, maintaining situational awareness, and preparing mentally for a sudden attack. It also covers everyday precautions such as locking doors, keeping windows closed, maintaining a full fuel tank, using mirrors, varying driving routes, and avoiding predictable routines. The final section reviews the roadblock-ramming procedure.

00:00 - The film introduces the threat of terrorist abductions and assassinations, noting that trained drivers can use specific techniques to survive an ambush.

1:46 - Proper mental conditioning and offensive driving give targets an advantage, demonstrating how a small sedan can defensively stop a larger vehicle.

3:07 - Chauffeur psychology prioritizes occupant safety over the car, utilizing the weight and heavy construction of American sedans as defensive assets.

3:53 - Vehicle speed, angle, and impact point determine mobility after a crash. Drivers must anticipate threats and prepare a response before an ambush.

4:22 - To counter a stationary roadblock, drivers should slow down, downshift, and brake suddenly to disorient attackers before choosing an escape route.

5:02 - Aiming the front fender at the blocking vehicle's rear wheel and accelerating pivots it out of the way, creating a path to escape.

5:56 - Deliberately ramming a car is psychological hurdle, but seat belts and proper impact points protect occupants during emergency collisions.

6:25 - Drivers must anticipate hazards blocks ahead to counter sudden alley ambushes or two-car "rolling box" traps.

7:06 - Escaping a two-car trap involves ramming one vehicle into the other or driving directly through the center gap.

7:28 - During a rolling ambush on a curve, drivers should use mirrors and stay alert to passing vehicles with multiple occupants.

8:03 - Emergency braking forces an attacking car to overshoot, while reversing or ramming its rear can also break visual contact.

8:53 - Urban escapes include mounting curbs at narrow angles to prevent tire damage, while avoiding terrain hazards like soft ground.

9:38 - Drivers should avoid going around roadblocks or sideswiping, which risks exposing occupants or locking vehicles together.

11:06 - Keeping windows closed prevents attackers from reaching inside or throwing rocks, grenades, and Molotov cocktails.

This amateur made newsreel film, "Storm Wrecks Jersey Coast" shows the aftermath of a major coastal storm that hit the Jersey Shore, bringing destructive winds and unusually high tides that flood communities from New Jersey to New England. Most likely, the event shown was the Great Atlantic Hurricane of 1944, which struck on September 14 and roared up the Eastern Seaboard, tearing away boardwalks, destroying homes, and damaging beachfront structures from Asbury Park all the way down to Atlantic City. Here, the Asbury Park boardwalk is shown heavily damaged, power is knocked out to thousands of homes, and buildings like hotels and piers are flooded or partially destroyed. After the storm passes, the shoreline is left in ruins, with birds seen searching through debris along the beach.

00:00 – A severe coastal storm hits the Jersey Shore, with strong winds and raging flood tides sweeping across the eastern seaboard. The storm is described as one of the worst in years, causing extensive and costly damage to coastal communities.0:27 – In Asbury Park, New Jersey, the boardwalk is heavily battered by the storm. Debris is scattered across the area, and the casino building suffers structural damage, including a section of its roof being torn away by the force of the wind and water.0:36 – The storm intensifies as powerful gales push inland from the sea, driving abnormal tidal surges. Water levels rise dramatically, with tides reaching as much as five feet above normal, overwhelming low-lying coastal areas.0:44 – These extreme conditions affect a wide stretch of coastline, from southern New Jersey up through parts of New England, with multiple communities experiencing flooding, erosion, and infrastructure damage.0:50 – Utility systems are severely disrupted when the Jersey Central Power and Light Company in Asbury Park experiences a major failure. As a result, approximately 10,000 homes lose electricity, along with access to radios and television, cutting off communication and information.0:58 – Additional flooding impacts local infrastructure, including hotels and public areas. The North End Hotel has its basement inundated, while in Ocean Grove, sections of the boardwalk are washed away, further highlighting the widespread coastal destruction.1:01 – The storm conditions begin to subside, leaving behind damaged landscapes and disrupted communities. Residual effects of flooding and debris remain across the shoreline.2:17 – In the aftermath, small beach animals—described as beach combers—move along the shoreline searching for food among the wreckage left by the storm, illustrating the ecological impact of the disaster.

“Radio Tubes” is a somewhat fragmentary, late 1920’s silent educational film providing explanation on functions of the radio tube. The film captures a point in early radio history when rapid innovations were taking place. It includes footage of a Fleming type tube, early portable radios including the RCA Radiola 26 Portable Super-Heterodyne, oscillators and large radio telephone transmitters. In the 1920’s radio tubes, also known as ‘vacuum tubes’, were replacing crystal sets. The film also explores crystal detectors using a galena crystal, how oscillators produce radio frequency currents as well as the transmission of images using wireless telegraphy systems. It also shows the sending of photographs by wire, aka wirephoto, telephotography, or radiophoto. This process, which became prominent in the 1920s, allowed news agencies to transmit images over telephone, telegraph, or radio lines, significantly speeding up the delivery of visual news to newspapers across the country. 

0:00 Film opens with a Fleming valve type radio tube (:22). These were considered to be the first thermionic vacuum tube invented by John Fleming in 1904. The tube acted as a detector for radio waves as it converted alternating currents of radio signals into a direct current. A series of title cards and diagrams begin to explain processes occurring within the tube. The filament is heated by electricity created by a battery (:33). Type “A” batteries powered the filaments, while “B” batteries enabled a stronger voltage for the plates. The location of the filament (:36), battery (:42) and vacuum are highlighted (:46). Electrons are thrown from the heated filament (:56). A plate surrounds the filament (1:04) connected to it’s battery (1:12). The plate holds a positive charge (1:17). Negatively charged electrons move towards the positively charged plate (1:32). Footage shows the current flowing in one direction due to the arrangement (1:37). A grid is set between the filament and plate (1:54). A diagram shows the new arrangement (2:10) noting location of the grid (2:15) and grid batteries (2:19). Weak currents produce a negative grid (2:23). Strong plate currents enable a positive grid (2:30). Currents are amplified through properly connected tubes (3:08). Credits acknowledge Western Electric Co. of NYC and RCA (3:22). Western operated from 1869 to 1996 as a subsidiary of AT&T. They were the primary manufacturer, supplier and purchasing agent for Bell System’s telephone equipment. RCA is a company with significant history founded in 1919 in an effort to monopolize the emerging radio industry. Examples feature a situation where the waves of a broadcast station are cut off (3:26) and where the radio frequency is induced in an aerial circuit (3:46). Another example shows the crystal detector (4:09) using a galena crystal (4:15). Crystal sets were popular and cheap for consumers. They would become obsolete by the mid-1920’s replaced by the vacuum tube and it’s powerful amplification abilities. The current flows in one direction through the crystal (4:26). Currents pulsating through “phones” (5:05) produce sound waves (5:10). A man and woman tune their RCA Radiola 26 Portable Super-Heterodyne radio (5:30). This was considered to be the first truly portable radio and weighed 25 lbs. Footage shows the radio tubes within (5:48). The oscillator produces radio frequency currents beginning with the power source connected to the oscillator (5:57). Oscillators enabled the selection of desired stations and were used as transmitters to create a carrier wave for broadcasting purposes. Amplification of oscillator output (6:47) and the effect of the addition of an Audion (8:05). Radio equipment used to transmit photographs (8:23).

This silent film "The Days of Steam on the L. & N." features footage shot by filmmaker Gene Miller in the mid-1930s through the 1950s. It shows the Louisville and Nashville Railroad's operations in Indiana and southwestern Kentucky.  The railroad began operating diesel locomotives in 1939 and stopped operating steam locomotives in 1957. The last steam locomotive to run on the line was a J-4 class 2-8-2 Mikado, number 1882. This film shows some of the progression in steam technology that occurred during the 20th Century, in that it ends with footage of one of the railroad's two streamlined trains. It also shows engines built at the Kentucky Locomotive Works in Louisville. The Works constructed a substantial number of steam engines including 31 classes of Consolidation 2-8-0s. 

0:00 Main titles. Locomotive 1040 shown at 2:13 is one of the H-23 class Consolidation engines. At 2:46, #1191 is an H-25 class built by Rogers in 1907. At 3:10 locomotive #1259 of the H-27A class arrives in Louisville. This engine was built by the L.& N. shops. The car shown at 3:35 is apparently a "Jim Crow" type passenger car. This was a segregated railroad car designated for Black passengers during the era of Jim Crow laws in the United States, which enforced racial segregation and required separate but unequal accommodations. At 3:41, #1303 from the Kentucky Locomotive Works built in 1911. At 4:04, 0-6-0 switch locomotive 2079 built by Rogers is shown. At 5:00, L.&N.'s first 0-8-0 switch locomotive #2114 is shown at Evansville.  At 6:34, a Pacific type K-4 4-6-2 is shown, number #230, pulling a passenger train. This is followed by engine No. 239, another K-4 fitted with 69-inch drivers and built in 1918. At 7:54, a K-5 locomotive #242 is shown at Evansville, built by the Richmond Locomotive Works. This engine had 73-inch drivers. At 8:41, locomotive #260 is shown crossing the Ohio River bridge at Henderson, Kentucky; this was a K-48 built by the Kentucky Locomotive Works in 1922. At 9:08, K-5 #270 is shown, built by Baldwin in 1923 and pictured at Howell, Indiana. At 9:52, 4-6-2 engine #272 is shown at Evansville, this was built by Brooks in 1924. It hauls a passenger train with multiple Pullman cars. At 10:36, engine #275 is shown. This K-5 was equipped with a bigger tender than available previously, to extend range between water stops. This engine was streamlined in 1940 and assigned the name "South Wind". At 11:09 the engine is seen pulling the Dixie Flagler passenger train on the trestle across the Ohio River at Henderson, Kentucky. At 11:46 it is seen at Sebree, Kentucky. 

The Louisville and Nashville Railroad, commonly called the L&N, was a Class I railroad that operated freight and passenger services in the southeast United States. Chartered by the Commonwealth of Kentucky in 1850, the road grew into one of the great success stories of American business. Operating under one name continuously for 132 years, it survived the Civil War and Great Depression and waves of social and technological change. Under Milton H. Smith, president of the company for 30 years, the L&N grew from a road with less than three hundred miles of track to a 6,000-mile system serving fourteen states. The L&N eventually extended its reach to St. Louis, Memphis, Atlanta, and New Orleans. The railroad was economically strong throughout its lifetime, earning the nickname, "The Old Reliable".  In the 1970s the railroad became a subsidiary of the Seaboard Coast Line Railroad and within a decade it was absorbed entirely.

These silent newsreels were created by Off Network Productions, a New York company created by producer and media magnate Gerald Bartell, using an archive compiled by Merton Koplin. The company distributed these films to TV stations around the United States, where they were used as fillers, and to present historical events and personalities to the public. Bartell referred to the films as a "visual encyclopedia". 

0:00 Film 1083: St Patrick's Day annual parade, New York City, 1957. Includes comments at :44 by the Mayor of Dublin Robert Briscoe who wears the Lord Mayor Chain of King William of Orange. Briscoe was a member of the Fianna Fáil political party and was the first Jewish person to hold the position of Lord Mayor. 
1:49 Film 1084: John Foster Dulles speaks about Communism in 1957.  This was Dulles first major foreign policy speech of the second Eisenhower administration to the associated press annual luncheon at the Waldorf Astoria Hotel. In his half hour speech, Dulles argued that the USA is the only free world country able to pay the cost of deterring the Soviet Union. 
3:33 Film 1085 Johnny Dio testifies in front of Congress about James Hoffa. Giovanni Ignazio Dioguardi, known as John "Johnny Dio" Dioguardi, was an Italian-American organized crime figure and a labor racketeer. He is known for being involved in the acid attack which led to the blinding of newspaper columnist Victor Riesel, and for his role in creating fake labor union locals to help Jimmy Hoffa become General President of the Teamsters. Beginning in 1955, the Permanent Subcommittee on Investigations of the U.S. Senate Committee on Government Operations began holding hearings into labor racketeering. Senator John L. McClellan, chair of the committee and chair of the subcommittee, hired Robert F. Kennedy as the subcommittee's chief counsel and investigator. Dioguardi became an object of the subcommittee's inquiries in March 1956.
4:44 Film 1088: President Dwight Eisenhower State Of The Union address, January 10, 1957, and makes comments about the economy and agricultural sector.
6:06 Film 1094: President Dwight Eisenhower, October 16, 1958, condemns Confederate Underground bombers of synagogues as “gangsters”. "From babyhood I was raised to respect the word ‘Confederate’ very highly, I might add, and for hoodlums such as these to describe themselves as any part or any relation to the Confederacy of the mid-19th Century is, to my mind, a complete insult to the word. Indeed, they should be described as nothing but Al Capones and Baby Face Nelsons and that kind of hoodlum." Note: Between November 11, 1957, and October 14, 1958, there were five bombings and three attempted bombings of synagogues, seven in the Southern United States and one in the Midwest United States. There were no deaths or injuries. White supremacists, such as the Confederate Underground, were opposed to Jewish support for integration and believed that integration was a Jewish plot to ruin America.
7:33 Film 1091: World Series 1957  New York Yankees vs. Milwaukee Braves. This was the 54th edition of the World Series, it was a best-of-seven playoff that matched the American League (AL) champion and defending World Series champion New York Yankees against the National League (NL) champion Milwaukee Braves; the Braves won the series in four games.

This short promo film from circa 1974 introduces Digital Equipment Corp's (DEC) Components Group, a specialized hardware business created for technically experienced customers who no longer required Digital's installation and service package. The group offers printers, magnetic tape systems, terminals, logic modules, and microcomputers on an unbundled basis, allowing customers to purchase in volume, install and maintain it themselves, to reduce costs. It also highlights DEC's educational programs, which trained more than 20,000 students and prepared customers to work independently. With warehouses in Massachusetts and Arizona and a separate operation in Marlboro, Mass., the Components Group reflects the growing diversification and commercialization of the minicomputer industry. It was formed by vice president Andrew C. Knowles. The film includes images of the PDP1140 introduced in 1973.

0:00 - Digital Equipment Corporation (DEC) introduces the range of specialized services supporting its position as a leader in the minicomputer industry. The film highlights DEC's education programs as an important part of these services.

0:16 - Footage shows a school established and operated by Digital as part of its educational program. DEC notes that more than 20,000 students attended Digital schools during the previous year, including prospective customers who gained enough technical knowledge to eventually manage their own systems without relying on DEC's additional services.

0:30 - The film explains that customers who have become familiar with Digital equipment can purchase hardware through the company's new Components Group and handle installation and servicing themselves.

0:41 - DEC describes the Components Group as an option for customers who need only the basic computer hardware and systems components. Instead of purchasing a complete package with Digital's installation and service support, customers can provide those functions themselves.

chapters.label: Digital Equipment Corporation (DEC) introduces the range of specialized services supporting its position as a leader in the minicomputer industry. The film highlights DEC's education programs as an important part of these services.

Footage shows a school established and operated by Digital as part of its educational program. DEC notes that more than 20,000 students attended Digital schools during the previous year, including prospective customers who gained enough technical knowledge to eventually manage their own systems without relying on DEC's additional services.
The film explains that customers who have become familiar with Digital equipment can purchase hardware through the company's new Components Group and handle installation and servicing themselves.

DEC describes the Components Group as an option for customers who need only the basic computer hardware and systems components. Instead of purchasing a complete package with Digital's installation and service support, customers can provide those functions themselves.

By selling components in volume without the additional service package, Digital says it can offer equipment at a lower cost while maintaining the reliability associated with its size and manufacturing experience.

DEC presents the Components Group as a logical development for experienced customers, emphasizing the division of responsibilities with the slogan, in effect, that customers know their own businesses while Digital knows computer equipment.

The Components Group is designed to provide unbundled peripheral equipment to users of different computer systems, expanding beyond the traditional approach of selling complete computer systems together with installation and service.

Examples of available equipment include printers, magnetic tape systems, alphanumeric terminals, remote data-entry terminals, solid-state logic modules, microcomputers, and other computer-related components. The variety illustrates the group's role as a hardware supplier rather than a full-service systems provider.

DEC emphasizes the potential savings of the new arrangement: customers purchase the equipment, install it themselves, and provide their own service, keeping the difference in cost that would otherwise go toward additional services.

The company describes its distribution operation, with Components Group equipment shipped in large-volume orders from Digital warehouses in Massachusetts and Arizona. The nationwide warehouse network is presented as another advantage of DEC's manufacturing and distribution scale.
DEC has established the new operation separately at One Iron Way in Marlboro, Massachusetts, a location associated with the company's operations in the area.

The Components Group is a new money-saving service made possible by Digital's experience in the computer industry. DEC promotes its components as reliable additions capable of improving and expanding customers' existing computer systems.
